f: Produced by Desta for Africa, directed by Aida Muluneh. The last sponsor list is from 2018: Swiss Embassy, Canon, National Geographic Society, Marriott and others. None published since.

f: Owned and run by the Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy, the government body that runs Rwanda's national museums.
w: Opened in 2009 in the former presidential palace at Kanombe and renamed the Rwanda Art Museum in 2018.

f: Artist-run centre founded in 2012 by painter brothers Innocent Nkurunziza and Emmanuel Nkuranga.
w: Ten resident-artist slots at KG 563 St, Kacyiru. A funder list is not published.

f: Won Culture Resource's Abbara Program grant (round 7, 2022). The Australian Government and Creative Australia support its Qubit fellowship (2026). The Spanish Embassy is a named partner.

w: Exhibitions change each quarter, showing Mauritian, Indian and South African artists, at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis.

f: Operates under the Women's Gallery Arts and Research Trust. Its March 2023 show had support from the Swiss and Australian embassies and UN Women. No funder list is published.

w: Opened 6 January 2023 in New Chamba Valley with a gallery, library and artist residency; first show Prospice, Kwacha!

f: Artists' association with over 100 members. State funding ended in the civil war; a late-1990s profile names Hivos as donor. No current funder list is published.

f: Binational centre under Namibian law, funded by the French government. Namibia gave the land and France paid for the building; foundation stone laid in 1998.
w: Has a large multipurpose gallery and hosts exhibitions at 118 Robert Mugabe Avenue, Windhoek.

n: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
f: Statutory museum set up by Act of Parliament in 1967 and run by the Department of National Museum and Monuments. Government funded its P33 million refurbishment, begun in 2020.
w: Includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery. Opened to the public in 1968.

n: Musée des Cultures Contemporaines Adama Toungara (MuCAT)
f: Built on the initiative of Adama Toungara, then mayor of Abobo; the director says it was built from own funds.
w: Stands opposite Abobo town hall on 3,500 m², designed by architect Issa Diabaté. Opened with the pan-African show Prête-moi ton rêve.

n: Festival International des Arts du Bénin (FInAB)
f: Run by Groupe Empire's events arm with Benin government support through its arts fund (FDAC). MTN partnered the 2026 edition, Canal+ Impact 2025. Other partners unnamed; no budget published.
w: Festival in Cotonou, Porto-Novo and Ouidah. The fourth edition closed in early March 2026, with days for Nigeria, Togo, Lebanon and Morocco.

f: Founded by Andrew Munuwa with Valentin Rudloff.
w: Launched in 2023. The 2025 edition showed 15 artists from Congo, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar.

f: Texaf, listed on Euronext Brussels, is founder and head sponsor of the centre. Its income is 85% Kinshasa real estate, 12% a sandstone quarry and 3% digital.
w: Texaf is 62.9% held by Société Financière Africaine and 10% by the Cha family. Bilembo covers over 1,000 m² of exhibition and workshop space.

f: Burkina Faso's culture ministry organises it and pays professional artists' fees, flights and stay, per its 2024 call for applications. No other funder is named.

n: Javett Art Centre at the University of Pretoria (Javett-UP)

f: Art network and incubator tied to the KNUST painting and sculpture department in Kumasi.
w: Ranked 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100 and invited to the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition.

f: Funded by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism as a level-1 public welfare institution. The Art Newspaper counted 7.4 million visitors in 2019.
w: Formed 2003 by merging the Museum of the Chinese Revolution and the National Museum of Chinese History. Building opened 1959.

f: Founded 1985 by the Nanjing Municipal Government; the Jiangsu provincial government added a research institute in 2016. The Standard reported about 6 million visitors in 2025.

n: Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance Against Japanese Aggression
f: Budget unit in the Beijing government's published accounts: 809 million yuan of public funding in 2025, 711 million of it project spending.
w: Inside Wanping Fortress near the Marco Polo Bridge. Beijing opened a patriotic education base there for Hong Kong and Macau youth in August 2025.

f: Run under county-level administration since 1984. Provincial permission was needed for exhibit changes in 1988 (Ho and Li, Modern China, 2016).
w: The 114 clay figures were made in 1965 by Sichuan Fine Arts Institute artists. Tens of millions visited in the Mao era.

f: Run by Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, which lists it among its institutions. Foreign adults pay $5 and Cambodians enter free, the museum states.
w: Former Khmer Rouge prison S-21. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 as part of the Cambodian Memorial Sites.

n: National Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Holy Defense
f: Tehran municipality built it, and its statute makes the municipality responsible for the budget and staff. The museum reported about 300,000 visitors a year (AFP, 2018).
w: Opened in 2012 in Tehran's Abbas-Abad cultural district. The Armed Forces General Staff published its statute amendments in 2021.

n: Museo Casa sobre el Arroyo (Casa del Puente)
f: The national state bought the house in 2012 and passed it to the city. The Ministry of Public Works paid over ARS 72M for the restoration, reopened April 2023.
w: Amancio Williams's house of 1943 to 1945 over the Las Chacras stream. Its restoration won the 2024 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize.

f: Lothar Trierenberg, of an Upper Austrian paper family, bought the house for EUR 5M and spent twice that restoring it. Stadt Wien gave EUR 700k, the Monuments Office about 200k.
w: Josef Frank and Oskar Wlach's 1930 villa, open since March 2026. Lothar Trierenberg co-owns delfortgroup, a specialty paper maker whose lines include cigarette paper.

f: Owned by the NSW Government and run by Museums of History NSW (successor to the Historic Houses Trust), a statutory body with a 2024-25 budget of A$73.6M.
w: Harry Seidler's 1950 house for his parents, handed to the state in 1988 and open to the public since 1991.

f: Robin Boyd Foundation revenue AUD 435k in 2023-24: donations 137k, grants 36k, partnerships 30k. Partners include Brickworks, Maddocks and Arup; donor trusts include Mori Provan and Isaacson Davis.
w: Robin Boyd's own 1959 house in South Yarra. A private ancillary foundation, unnamed, lent AUD 1.8M interest free against the title.

f: Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club is funded by Stadt Wien, Bezirk Margareten, the federal arts ministry, GESIBA and arching. ORF named Wertinvest, the building's owner, a financial backer in 2021.
w: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.
why: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.

f: STEINHAUS Günther Domenig Privatstiftung receives subsidies from Land Kärnten (culture) and the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport. Gemeinde Steindorf and HTL Villach give in-kind sponsoring.

f: The commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961. The museum's EUR 800k renewal is paid by Urban Brussels, the commune, Fonds Baillet-Latour, museum resources and an unnamed patron.
w: Victor Horta's house and studio of 1898 to 1901, a museum since 1969. The first phase of facade and reception works ends in November 2026.

f: Run by the Boghossian Foundation, created in 1992 by the jewellers Robert Boghossian and his sons, which bought and restored the villa. The Circle of the Villa adds donors.
w: Michel Polak's villa of 1930, an art centre since 2010. Circle donors include Jan-Leonard Moortgat (Duvel) and Claude Moët (Moët & Chandon).

w: Garden tours run April to October and the house interior is closed. Phyllis Lambert chairs a board of 16 directors.

f: Donations were CZK 4.48M in 2025: CZK 4.40M from founder Bata Schuh Stiftung, CZK 30k from Continental Barum. Subsidies: City of Zlín CZK 195k, Zlín Region CZK 35k.
w: Thomas J. Bata recovered the villa by restitution and donated it to the foundation. Rosemarie Bata Blyth chairs the board, which includes Zlín's mayor.

f: The National Heritage Institute runs it. Transfers, mostly from the Ministry of Culture, were 69 percent of 2024 revenue. EU's ERDF paid 85 percent of a CZK 179M restoration project.
w: Built 1927 to 1929 for textile owner Alfred Stiassni and later used for state visits, including Fidel Castro's. Opened to the public in December 2014.

f: The Brummel family owns the house. Plzeň - TURISMUS, a City of Pilsen organisation, runs the tours. The Adolf Loos Plzeň project credits Ministry for Regional Development state-budget money.
w: Jan and Jana Brummel commissioned Loos to remodel the house in 1929. Their nephew Michal took it over in 1991.

f: Herita vzw, a heritage non-profit, runs it with the City of Antwerp. The Flemish Government set EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year under a one-year agreement.

w: The US State Department and Treasury authorised the foundation's 2015 shipment of four containers for an on-site conservation workshop.

f: Opened 18 January 1992 by the Office of the City Historian of Havana with Oswaldo Guayasamín. Original works donated to the Cuban nation are on show.
w: Housed in an 18th-century house at Obrapía 111, where restoration uncovered colonial mural paintings.
why: Housed in an 18th-century house at Obrapía 111, where restoration uncovered colonial mural paintings.

n: Oficina del Historiador de la Ciudad de La Habana
f: Runs on the state budget and other authorised sources (Decree-Law 368, 2018). Its deputy director said in 2024 that large companies still hand over their historic-centre profits.
w: GAESA took over its business companies, led by Habaguanex, in 2016. Habaguanex, Hoteles Habaguanex, Fénix and GAESA are on the US Cuba Restricted List.
why: GAESA took over its business companies, led by Habaguanex, in 2016. Habaguanex, Hoteles Habaguanex, Fénix and GAESA are on the US Cuba Restricted List.

n: Museo de la Ciudad de La Habana
f: Housed in the Palace of the Captains General, the seat of the Office of the City Historian of Havana from 1938. The Office opened its first rooms in 1968.
w: Occupies the 1776 to 1791 palace on Plaza de Armas. The Historian's Office claims 40 permanent exhibition rooms.
why: Occupies the 1776 to 1791 palace on Plaza de Armas. The Historian's Office claims 40 permanent exhibition rooms.

n: Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso
f: State theatre run by the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, under the Ministry of Culture. Reopened in 2016 after a three-year restoration; new repairs were under way in 2025.
w: Home of the Ballet Nacional de Cuba. The council's president named roof, air-conditioning and vibration damage behind the 2025 repair.
nodes: Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas

f: Founded in 1948 by Alicia Alonso and paid by the Cuban state. The British Friends of Ballet Nacional de Cuba, a UK charity, exist to fund equipment and new productions.
w: Down to 55 dancers in 2025 from over 100 at times, as members took jobs abroad (New York Times).
nodes: British Friends of Ballet Nacional de Cuba

f: State theatre run by the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas under the Ministry of Culture. Built from 1951 and opened in 1979; its two halls seat 2,254 and 805.
w: Its Sala Avellaneda hosted the opening concert of the 41st Jazz Plaza festival in January 2026.

f: Film archive and cinema programme created in 1960 as a department of ICAIC, which sits in the Ministry of Culture. It moved into Alfredo Guevara's former house in October 2020.
w: Member of the International Federation of Film Archives (FIAF). ICAIC, its parent, carries the censorship and protest flags.

n: Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos (ICAIC)
f: State film body created by Law No. 169 in 1959, funded through the Ministry of Culture. It runs the Cinemateca, the Havana film festival, the Muestra Joven and animation studios.
w: Films pulled: Regreso a Ítaca 2014, Santa y Andrés 2016, Sueños al pairo 2020. In 2023 the Asamblea de Cineastas Cubanos denounced ICAIC censorship.
why: State film body created by Law No. 169 in 1959, funded through the Ministry of Culture. It runs the Cinemateca, the Havana film festival, the Muestra Joven and animation studios.

n: Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano de La Habana
f: Annual December festival organised by ICAIC, a Ministry of Culture body, since 1979. Its founder Alfredo Guevara chaired it until his death in 2013.
w: In December 2023 the Asamblea de Cineastas Cubanos said Llamadas desde Moscú and La Habana de Fito were pulled. Regreso a Ítaca: 2014.

n: Universidad de las Artes de Cuba (ISA)
f: State university in the Ministry of Culture system. Italy agreed in February 2019 to give 2.5 million euros to renovate the theatre faculty and fund teaching and events.
w: Its theatre faculty building is a national monument; the National Art Schools complex was on the World Monuments Fund watch list in 2000 and 2016.
nodes: State university in the Ministry of Culture system

n: Unión de Escritores y Artistas de Cuba (UNEAC)
f: Membership union founded in 1961 that runs galleries, magazines and the Premios Caracol, given since 1978. Its 2020 statutes list dues, a state contribution and donations as income.
w: UNEAC expelled historian Alina Bárbara López on 12 September 2024 for criticising Revolution leaders. Writer Jorge Fernández Era quit in solidarity before 18 September.
why: Membership union founded in 1961 that runs galleries, magazines and the Premios Caracol, given since 1978. Its 2020 statutes list dues, a state contribution and donations as income.

n: Biblioteca Nacional de Cuba José Martí
f: State library in the Ministry of Culture system and head of the national public library network. Declared a National Monument on 30 June 2021.
w: Contributes digitised material to the Digital Library of the Caribbean, which holds a Celebrating Cuba collection built with other partners.
nodes: State library in the Ministry of Culture system

n: Feria Internacional del Libro de La Habana
f: Book fair held since 1982, annual since 2000, run by the Instituto Cubano del Libro, a Ministry of Culture body. The 34th edition opened in August 2026 after a postponement.
w: The 34th edition honoured the centenary of Fidel Castro's birth, had Russia as guest country and moved to Línea y 18 from La Cabaña.

f: State record company founded in 1964, in the Ministry of Culture system. Sony Music has distributed its albums abroad since 2015; Sony/ATV has licensed its songs since January 2018.
w: A 2017 study by Cuba's music research centre, cited by Wikipedia, gave EGREM 58 percent of Cuban digital music revenue in 2016.
nodes: Sony Music has distributed its albums abroad

f: Annual January jazz festival first held in 1980 and organised by the Instituto Cubano de la Música. The 42nd edition is set for 24 to 31 January 2027.
w: Holguín was announced as a venue for the 41st edition (Prensa Latina, November 2025). Organisers say over 120 US artists have confirmed for 2027.
nodes: Annual January jazz festival first held

f: Screening of young Cuban directors' films run by ICAIC with a filmmakers' board. The 19th edition, set for April 2020, was postponed; 14ymedio wrote in 2025 that it had disappeared.
w: 2018: ICAIC moved one film to a 24-seat room; the director withdrew it. 2020: ICAIC cut a documentary and at least six filmmakers withdrew works.

n: Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión (EICTV)
c: San Antonio de los Baños, Cuba
f: The Cuban government supported it at founding. Tuition was 5,000 euros a year in 2011 (AFP). EU-financed UNESCO Transcultura supplied equipment and courses valued at 600,000 euros in 2024.
w: The school's site lists the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC as supporters. In 2026 it also runs a donation campaign for energy autonomy.

f: Founded in 1899 by Santiago's mayor Emilio Bacardí, this state museum got its building in 1927 from his widow Elvira Cape. The Ministry of Culture's provincial heritage centre oversees it.
w: National Monument since 1999. OnCuba reports more than 23,000 items in three halls and an art annex.

n: Museo Castillo del Morro San Pedro de la Roca
f: Cuban state property; UNESCO names the Consejo Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural as responsible agency. A museum opened in the fortress on 23 July 1978. State bodies began repairs in 2020.
w: UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997. Granma, quoted by OnCuba in April 2021, reported the repairs would continue through 2021.

f: Private studio-gallery founded in Havana in 1995 by curator Cristina Vives and photographer José A. Figueroa. It describes itself as self-financed; the Norwegian Embassy in Cuba is a named collaborator.
w: Founders say the private studio has no legal support and faces hostility. Dialogue with state institutions has been on and off and one-way (IPS, 2020).
nodes: CRAC Valparaíso (Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo)

f: Open as a museum since 1974, the Palacio Brunet is an 1808 mansion restored from 1964. The Sancti Spíritus heritage centre's 2024 summer programme includes this state museum.
w: The Asociación Pro Trinidad bought the palace in 1945. Trinidad's historic centre has been on the UNESCO list since 1988.

f: Opened in 1955 in a former cavalry barracks, Camagüey's provincial museum is a state institution. A private Patronato Pro Museo assembled its first collection.
w: Holds Cuban painting including Wifredo Lam and Amelia Peláez, plus natural history and decorative arts rooms.

f: State theatre in Cienfuegos, a National Monument. Built 1887 to 1890 with 115,000 gold pesos set aside by the heirs of slave-owning sugar planter Tomás Terry.
w: The building won the National Conservation Prize in 2008. Spanish Wikipedia lists it among eight large colonial-era theatres.

f: Matanzas state theatre, a National Monument since 1978, closed 2010 to 2018 for restoration (EcuRed: 2019). Its main hall closed mid-2024; ACN said in July 2025 it would reopen.
w: The state heritage council gave the restoration its 2020 National Restoration Prize. Seating is 775.

c: San Antonio de los Baños, Cuba
f: Opened 17 March 1979 per EcuRed (14ymedio: 1948) in an 1830 house in San Antonio de los Baños; the Ministry of Culture is its parent body, per EcuRed.
w: Hosts the Bienal Internacional del Humor, whose 24th edition ran in April 2025 (Cubaperiodistas). EcuRed counts over 10,000 works from 40 countries.

n: American Museum of the Cuban Diaspora
f: Non-profit Cuban Museum Inc. A $10 million Miami-Dade County bond grant (2004) built it and county funds support it. The City of Miami added $175,000 in American Rescue Plan money.
w: In September 2017 seven of 13 county commissioners moved $550,000 from the Pérez Art Museum to this museum; Jorge Pérez called it punishment.
why: In September 2017 seven of 13 county commissioners moved $550,000 from the Pérez Art Museum to this museum; Jorge Pérez called it punishment.

f: Florida non-profit run by a volunteer board that says donations and volunteers maintain the building. State of Florida grants of $2.8 million paid for the restoration reopened in 1992.
w: Founded in 1871 by Cuban exiles. Cuba's government gave $80,000 for the 1920s rebuilding and paid a teacher's salary until 1959.

f: Independent art institute founded in 2015 and set up by a crowdfunding campaign of 915 backers. In 2024 its whole income, $95,283, came from Estudio Bruguera, the founder's studio.
w: Cuban authorities detained founder Tania Bruguera in December 2014 and January 2015; INSTAR says the street outside was drilled during its 2015 reading.

f: Non-profit educational institution founded in 1972 that runs the Cuban Art Space gallery. Its 2024 revenue was $296,120, of which $194,216 was contributions and $86,374 program services (Form 990).
w: Founded in 1972 to counter US policy toward Cuba. A bomb wrecked its New York premises on 28 March 1973; its letter named no perpetrator.

f: A building of 1860 to 1868 on Parque Calixto García houses Holguín's state provincial history museum, whose heritage centre lists six rooms; EcuRed says one is mounted.
w: National Monument since 10 October 1978. Spanish Wikipedia dates the museum to 1980, EcuRed to 25 July 1976.

n: Museo Provincial de Pinar del Río
f: State provincial history museum in a building that housed the provincial government from 1892 to 1959. It belongs to the Pinar del Río provincial heritage centre.
w: Opened with one room on 14 December 1979 and the rest in 1981. Rooms cover archaeology, history, decorative arts and local musicians.

n: Museo Provincial de Granma Manuel Muñoz Cedeño
f: Bayamo's provincial museum opened on 19 October 1982 as the Museo Histórico de Bayamo, in the city's historic centre. It belongs to the Centro Provincial de Patrimonio Cultural en Granma.
w: Armando Hart, then minister of culture, attended the opening. Bayamo's historic centre has been a National Monument since 1935, ratified in 1978.
